philosophyChapters.summary: Locke, Berkeley and Hume are often considered the three principal names of the British empiricist tradition. philosophyChapters.summary: Science is not just a list of facts. Science is a complex process of questioning, hypothesizing, observing, measuring, experimenting, calculating, modelling, theorizing, reproducing and institutionalizing inquiry. Individuals may be legally free, without real options due to hunger, debt, caste exclusion, patriarchy, illiteracy, violence, lack of disability-friendly structures, or societal fears. philosophyChapters.synthesis: Failure to support the statement and proving the statement is false are different situations. However, if the claim is true, conclusive evidence is expected, and if it is not found after an exhaustive search, the absence may constitute negative evidence.

philosophyChapters.title: The Problem of Suffering and Evil
philosophyChapters.summary: If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good, then why is there innocent suffering? It is one of the most difficult questions in philosophy. But the problem of evil is not just an intellectual conundrum. Disease, famine, violence, child-mortality, war, natural calamities and humiliation are the real sufferings. For this reason, the moral style of the philosophical answer is also important.

On the contrary, the problem cannot be eliminated by simply saying it is God 's plan.
philosophyChapters.synthesis: Whether the problem of evil is only suffering or not is relevant in so many ways, at so many times, and in so many senseless ways. Character can be created with little difficulty, but it is difficult to justify the extreme suffering of a child or animal with identical answers.

philosophyChapters.title: Karma, Rebirth, and Mokṣa
philosophyChapters.summary: Karma, reincarnation, and moksha are interrelated but not synonymous concepts in many traditions of Indian philosophy. The Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions differ profoundly on the nature of karma, the continuity of karta and rebirth, and the meaning of mukti. Therefore, it is not appropriate to present the same version of the Indian karma-principle text.

philosophyChapters.synthesis: If the present state is determined by past actions, what is the meaning of new actions and moral efforts? Most karma-views are not absolute determinism; rather, existing actions can give new directions by creating pre-causal circumstances.

philosophyChapters.title: Religious Plurality
philosophyChapters.summary: In the same world, there exist many religious traditions, many God-concepts, many paths to liberation, and many atheistic traditions. Secularism is not only a social fact; it is also an epistemological and moral question. If intelligent, honest, and studious individuals reach conflicting religious conclusions, what effect does this have on the certainty of their beliefs?

The first act of communication is to clarify the traditional function of the word. There may be different questions behind the same words and common problems behind different words.

philosophyChapters.title: Religion and the State
philosophyChapters.summary: The question of the relationship between religion and the state is not as simple as simply whether the state is religious or secular. The fundamental problem in a multi-religious society is whether the legitimacy of the state rests on the equal political status of all citizens or on the privilege of claiming a religious truth. Parallel philosophies do not command the state to be heretical; they do not give the state the right…

Religious individuals are able to give public reasons. a secular state is not an anti-religious state.

philosophyChapters.summary: Religious life is not confined to scriptures, monasteries, temples, mosques, churches, guilds or formal doctrines. In folk life, festivals, songs, stories, fasts, household rituals, local deities, rivers, trees, ancestors, seasons, diseases, cures, agriculture, and rites of passage have religious connotations. To dismiss this world as unscriptural would be to lose sight of a vast body of religious history. But it is also…

It is useful to find the original text, but not to think of the surviving versions as corrupted copies.

philosophyChapters.title: Modernity
philosophyChapters.summary: Modernism is not just a term for time. Science, industry, capitalism, nation-state, individualism, bureaucracy, democracy, mass education, colonialism, markets, printing, urbanization, and new communication systems are its different historical dimensions. It is difficult to make modernity the same source or the same value story.

Parallel philosophies choose between the knowledge of tradition without the injustice of tradition or the freedom of modernity without the dehumanization of modernity.
philosophyChapters.synthesis: Printing, assemblies, journals, and modern communication give private individuals a platform to argue public questions. But access may be limited by education, language, property, and gender; so-called public opinion may in fact be the opinion of a narrow group.

philosophyChapters.title: Science and the Human Being
philosophyChapters.summary: Science is one of the most powerful systems of knowledge in human history. Modern medicine was profoundly changed by communication, agriculture, energy, transportation, physics, and cosmology. But the power of scientific knowledge does not automatically give moral direction. What is possible and what should be done are different questions.

philosophyChapters.summary: Language is not only the naming of ready-made realities but also the means to classify social realities, visible and invisible. The names they give sometimes affect what society considers normal, deviant, criminal, or disease rights or identities. But this fact does not lead to the conclusion that reality is created only by language. The relationship between language and the world is a complex field of existence, experience,…

Not all evidence of what happened survives the same way. Royal court documents may be preserved, but not the experiences of agricultural labourers. Male genealogies may be written down. philosophyChapters.summary: Traditional morality focused mainly on the relationships between humans in the present. But the environmental crisis changes the question. I have a responsibility to the unborn generation The species is only a means for human use. The value of the river is only the market-value The decisions we make today have consequences that affect life hundreds of years from now.

The power is in the future, so is the responsibility.

philosophyChapters.summary: The first basic tenet of the parallel philosophy proposed in this text is that of multidimensional rationalism. This does not mean that all evidence is the same or that all beliefs can be true. It means that there is truth and knowledge is possible, but knowledge is not the only kind of evidence. philosophyChapters.summary: Another theory is that of coexistential realism. It starts with a rejection of the two extremes. Firstly, the world is only a construction of our consciousness or language; secondly, reality is only a lifeless mass of separate objects and not of any fundamental importance to relationships. philosophyChapters.title: Dignity-Based Ethics
philosophyChapters.summary: The moral center of Parallel Philosophy is dignity. Dignity means that the basic moral values of every human being precede birth, caste, sex, wealth, language, religion, ability, position, utility or acceptance by the majority. Man cannot be seen merely as a carrier of means, numbers, labour power, voters, consumers or community prestige.

philosophyChapters.title: Polycentric Democracy
philosophyChapters.summary: Democracy cannot be abolished by elections alone, nor by the institution of parliament or capital. The political doctrine of the Parallel Philosophy is multicentric democracy. This implies a possible decentralization of power, knowledge, resources, and decision-making but equal constitutional protection of fundamental rights.

philosophyChapters.summary: Parallel theology does not regard atheism as a moral vacuum, nor does it equate faith with superstition. Prudential pluralism means that different religious and non-religious views of life coexist with equal civic dignity, but the test of common propriety applies to public obligations.

people.name: Acharya Ramanand Mandal

His writing is analyzed through the Parallel History Framework as a voice of the "Jan Kavi" tradition, prioritizing the linguistic and social realities of the marginalized over Sanskritized academic norms.

people.name: Ajit Kumar Jha
people.description: Author of the reflective and autobiographical work Jatbe Bujhlahun Tatbe Likhlahun. His contributions are valued for their "unfiltered" pratyakṣa, offering a direct testimonial (śabda) of the contemporary Maithil experience.

people.name: Amit Mishra
people.description: A significant voice in the Maithili Ghazal revival. His work is noted for its adherence to the Behr (meter) and Qaafiyaa (rhyme) standards established by the Anchinhar movement.

people.name: Amod Kumar Jha
people.description: A poet, editor, and critic whose work integrates the Nāṭyaśāstra’s Rasa-Dhvani aesthetics with a modern, socially critical lens.

people.name: Anand Kumar Jha

people.name: Anmol Jha

people.name: Arvind Thakur
people.description: The subject of a significant special issue (Issue 438) edited by Ashish Anchinhar, focusing on his contributions to regional Maithili activism and prose.

people.name: Ashish Anchinhar

His theoretical work, Maithili Ghazalak Vyakarana o Itihasa, provided the first systematic grammar for the genre in Maithili. His poetry is characterized by Lāghava (logical parsimony) and a sharp focus on Dhvani.

people.name: Ashok
people.description: A multifaceted writer and editor. His works in the archive include Nava Kavita, the satire collection Neek Dinak Bioscope, and the critical study Katha-Path. His editing of the journals Sandhan and Pratiman is treated as an exercise in Pratyakṣa-based curation, favoring social realism over romanticized tropes.

people.name: Bechan Thakur
people.description: A pioneer of the Videha Maithili Parallel Theatre Movement. His work is analyzed through the lenses of Brecht, Boal, and the Nāṭyaśāstra, representing a "theatre from below" that challenges the elite Darbhanga-centric dramatic tradition.

people.name: Bhavnath Jha
people.description: A scholar, epigraphist, and manuscriptologist whose contributions to cultural preservation are documented in the Videha Bhavnath Jha Special Issue (Issue 427). His work is analyzed as a bridge between the traditional scholarship of the Navya-Nyāya logicians and modern digital archiving.

people.name: Binay Bhushan

people.name: Bindeshwar Thakur

people.name: Chandan Kumar Jha

people.name: Ilarani Singh

people.name: Jagdanand Jha "Manu"

people.name: Jagdish Prasad Mandal

people.name: Kailash Kumar Mishra

people.name: Kalikant Jha ‘Buch’

people.name: Kamini Kamayini

people.name: Kapileshwar Raut
people.description: A writer of stories that focus on the "ordinary" and "marginalized" rural Maithil, often featured in the Nit Naval series.

people.name: Kirtinath Jha
people.description: A physician and scholar whose translations of Tamil poetry (Kural) and Kahlil Gibran (Tootal Pankhi) have expanded the thematic horizons of Maithili literature. His original story collection, Kichhu Puran Gapp, Kichhu Nav Gapp, is noted for its technical discipline and restraint.

people.name: Kumar Manoj Kashyap
people.description: A contributor to contemporary Maithili prose whose work is characterized by its engagement with the "provincial-yet-cosmopolitan" experience of the Maithili diaspora.

people.name: Kusum Thakur
people.description: A memoirist and poet whose work provides a unique feminine perspective on the historical and familial structures of Mithila.

people.name: Lāl Dev Kāmat
people.description: A central figure in the democratized wave of Maithili literature. His primary works—Vibhṛiti, Divya Dṛiṣṭi, Gahiki Najari, and Sheṣ Jīvan—bridge the gap between literature and practical instruction. His work Vibhṛiti (2020) is particularly significant for its integration of organic farming techniques with literary prose poems, embodying the classical concept of lokahitakārī (people-benefiting) literature. Through the lens of…

people.name: Lallan Prasad Thakur
people.description: A playwright and actor whose contributions to the Parallel Theatre movement have helped preserve the folk motifs of Mithila in a modern dramatic context.

people.name: Laxman Jha ‘Sagar’
people.description: A Kolkata-based writer and activist whose five decades of work in poetry and short fiction act as an "embodied commitment" to the Maithili cause, especially within the industrial-commercial milieu of the diaspora.

people.name: Mala Jha
people.description: A writer of Maithili fiction whose works are often analyzed in the context of the evolving domestic and social roles of women in Mithila.

people.name: Meena Jha
people.description: A pioneer of Maithili social realism and women's medical fiction. Her landmark story on breast cancer is identified as the first in Maithili literature to treat this subject with such depth, predating similar Hindi fiction. Her work is a masterful application of Navya-Nyāya pratyakṣa, making speakable what social discourse had previously left unspoken (śabda).

people.name: Munni Kamat
people.description: A playwright known for the one-act play Jindagik Mol and other works that utilize theatre as a tool for social critique.

people.name: Munnaji
people.description: Featured in Part 74 of the Parallel History series for research contributions that integrate regional folklore with modern literary criticism.

people.name: Nagendra Kumar
people.description: A poet and scholar analyzed in the collective research of Part 96, recognized for his contribution to the intellectualization of Maithili verse.

people.name: Nand Kumar Mishra 'Nand'
people.description: A prolific author of novels, stories, and children's literature whose work spans multiple decades and reflects the changing socio-political landscape of Mithila.

people.name: Nand Vilas Roy
people.description: A storyteller and playwright whose contributions to the Nit Naval series highlight the resilience of the subaltern voice in the face of economic marginalization.

people.name: Om Prakash Jha
people.description: One of the "Three Voices of the Maithili Ghazal" analyzed in Part 79 for his mastery of ghazal prosody and his role in the form's revival.

people.name: Preeti Thakur
people.description: A pioneer of Maithili children's picture-story literature. Her work is analyzed through children's literature theory and the Parallel History framework, representing a critical intervention in the early literacy and cultural formation of Maithili-speaking children.

people.name: Premshankar Singh
people.description: A senior researcher and scholar whose work on the socio-literary history of Maithili has provided a foundation for contemporary parallel history studies.

people.name: Rajdeo Mandal
people.description: A Maithili writer whose poetry and novels represent the authentic subaltern voice. His work is central to the Parallel History series and is often analyzed as a form of "Archival Resistance" against canonical exclusions.

people.name: Ram Vilas Sahu
people.description: A storyteller whose works in the Nit Naval series are praised for their precise observation of rural life and their grounding in Navya-Nyāya pratyakṣa.

people.name: Ramesh Jha
people.description: A storyteller whose works explore the psychological and social complexities of the modern Maithil middle class, particularly in the context of migration and urban life.

people.name: Ramesh Narayan
people.description: Analyzed alongside other regional poets in Part 96 for his role in sustaining the tradition of Maithili lyricism.

people.name: Ravibhushan Pathak
people.description: A translator and researcher whose work in the Sadeha volumes focuses on bringing diverse Indian and international literary voices into the Maithili fold.

people.name: Satyanand Pathak
people.description: Author of Gaam Gel Chhalahun (The Village has Gone), a work that explores the "Dialectics of Displacement" and the loss of the traditional Maithil village structure.

people.name: Santosh Kumar Mishra
people.description: A poet and cultural activist whose work is analyzed for its integration of activist motifs with lyrical beauty.

people.name: Shiv Kumar Jha 'Tillu'
people.description: A poet and critic described as a "Cultural Witness" and a "Parallel Voice" of Mithila, whose work provides a lyrical record of social transitions.

people.name: Shivshankar Srinivas
people.description: A significant critic and author whose works like Maithili Upanyasak Alochana provide the theoretical framework for understanding the evolution of the Maithili novel.

people.name: Subhash Chandra Yadav
people.description: A central contemporary figure whose "complete literary works" have been archived and analyzed as part of the Nit Naval series, reflecting a commitment to linguistic purity and social realism.

people.name: Sujit Kumar Jha
people.description: A journalist and storyteller from Janakpurdham (Nepal). His work is a critical "Nepali-Maithili voice," offering insights into the cross-border cultural continuity of Mithila and the unique challenges faced by the community in the Terai region.

people.name: Taranand Viyogi
people.description: A critic and writer whose analysis, "Beyond the Rhetoric," challenges established literary narratives and focuses on the "fractured voice" of contemporary Maithili experience.

people.name: Udaya Narayana Singh ‘Nachiketa’
people.description: A polymath poet, playwright, and linguist whose contributions are analyzed for their formal innovation and their role in bridging Maithili with global linguistic theories.

people.name: Umesh Mandal
people.description: A poet, scholar, and digital pioneer whose work is central to the "democratized wave" of the Videha movement. His stories and critical appreciations are grounded in the epistemological demands of perceiving social truth.

people.name: Umesh Paswan
people.description: A Dalit voice in Maithili poetry and fiction. His work is analyzed through the lens of "Dalit Aesthetics" and Navya-Nyāya, representing a radical disruption of the historically brahminical Maithili canon.

people.name: Vibha Rani
people.description: A multifaceted researcher and writer whose work in the Parallel History series explores the intersections of folk traditions, women's performance, and modern realism.

people.name: Vijaynath Jha
people.description: A critic and researcher whose appreciations of contemporary Maithili literature focus on the synthesis of traditional Rasa theory with modern subaltern themes.

people.name: Vineet Utpal
people.description: A scholar and writer whose research on translation theory and the Parallel History framework has helped institutionalize the movement’s intellectual goals.

people.name: Yogendra Pathak Viyogi
people.description: A physicist and science-fiction pioneer who has expanded the thematic boundaries of Maithili literature to include scientific rationalism and speculative narratives.

people.name: Yājñavalkya
people.description: Debate on self, knowledge, negation, and liberation in the remembered court of Videha.

people.name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
people.description: Fearless questioning on the structure and limits of the cosmos in the Videha dialogue tradition.

people.name: Maitreyī
people.description: Interrogates wealth, love, selfhood, and immortality in dialogue with Yājñavalkya.

people.name: King Janaka
people.description: Remembered patron and interlocutor in the learned court traditions of Videha.

people.name: Udayanācārya
people.description: Mithila philosopher examined through Ātmatattvaviveka, Nyāyakusumāñjali, argument, and counterargument.

people.name: Vācaspati Miśra
people.description: Major commentator across philosophical schools; central to the Bhāmatī translation shelf.

people.name: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya
people.description: Author of Tattvacintāmaṇi and a foundational figure in Mithila's new logic.

people.name: Akṣapāda Gautama
people.description: Associated with the Nyāyasūtra tradition of proof, doubt, inference, debate, and error.

people.name: Kaṇāda
people.description: Associated with a realist analysis of substance, property, action, universal, particular, and inherence.

people.name: Kapila
people.description: Traditional figure linked with Sāṃkhya's analysis of consciousness, nature, and the tattvas.

people.name: Patañjali
people.description: Associated with disciplined inquiry into mind, suffering, practice, detachment, and liberation.

people.name: Jaimini
people.description: Associated with inquiry into injunction, language, testimony, action, and interpretive authority.

people.name: Bādarāyaṇa
people.description: Associated with the Brahmasūtras and later plural traditions of Vedānta commentary.

people.name: Śaṅkara
people.description: Advaita philosopher whose Brahmasūtra Bhāṣya forms the base text for the Bhāmatī tradition.

people.name: Rāmānuja
people.description: Represents a relational reading of unity within the Vedānta comparison.

people.name: Madhva
people.description: Represents a realist insistence on difference in the disciplined plurality of Vedānta.

people.name: The Buddha
people.description: Placed within the eastern Gangetic world of suffering, dependent arising, ethics, and liberation.

people.name: Nāgārjuna
people.description: Central to the inquiry into emptiness, dependence, conceptual limits, and the middle way.

people.name: Dignāga
people.description: A key figure in Buddhist pramāṇa theory and the analysis of perception and inference.

people.name: Dharmakīrti
people.description: Develops disciplined accounts of proof, inference, and reliable cognition.

people.name: Mahāvīra
people.description: Linked with the eastern Gangetic setting of nonviolence, plurality, karma, and liberation.

people.name: Bharata Muni
people.description: The Nāṭyaśāstra supplies a framework for performance, rasa, theatre, and critical appreciation.

people.name: Ānandavardhana
people.description: Dhvani theory supports readings of suggestion and aesthetic meaning in Maithili literature.

people.name: Abhinavagupta
people.description: His rasa and dhvani interpretation informs the archive's synthesis of Indian criticism.

people.name: Kuntaka
people.description: Vakrokti theory supplies a vocabulary for oblique expression and literary distinctiveness.

people.name: Mammaṭa
people.description: A classical theorist engaged in discussions of poetic qualities, faults, and aesthetic analysis.

people.name: Vidyāpati
people.description: A central, contested figure read across Maithili, Sanskrit, court, devotion, law, and parallel history.

people.name: Jyotiriśvara Ṭhākura
people.description: Associated with Varṇaratnākara and the early literary world of Karnata-period Mithila.

people.name: Umapati Upādhyāya
people.description: A literary figure situated within the long history of Maithili performance and dramatic writing.

people.name: Harimohan Jha
people.description: A major modern writer whose satire and critique of orthodoxy are foregrounded by the Parallel History.

people.name: George A. Grierson
people.description: A colonial-era linguistic scholar whose classifications require both use and critical contextualization.

people.name: Rahul Sankrityayan
people.description: Appears within wider debates over language, manuscripts, travel, history, and eastern Indian intellectual culture.

people.name: Socrates
people.description: Represents questioning, examination, and the ethical demand to give reasons.

people.name: Plato
people.description: Examined through dialogue, knowledge, justice, forms, and political philosophy.

people.name: Aristotle
people.description: Engaged across logic, causality, ethics, politics, and comparative poetics.

people.name: René Descartes
people.description: Represents methodic doubt and the modern search for certainty.

people.name: Baruch Spinoza
people.description: Examined through substance, reason, freedom, and the critique of superstition.

people.name: G. W. Leibniz
people.description: Engaged through rationalism, plurality, sufficient reason, and the problem of evil.

people.name: John Locke
people.description: Examined through experience, personal identity, rights, and political legitimacy.

people.name: George Berkeley
people.description: Part of the inquiry into perception, ideas, and the status of the external world.

people.name: David Hume
people.description: A critical voice on causation, induction, self, religion, and the limits of proof.

people.name: Immanuel Kant
people.description: Engaged through limits of knowledge, autonomy, dignity, and the conditions of judgment.

people.name: G. W. F. Hegel
people.description: A major interlocutor on history, recognition, contradiction, and dialectical method.

people.name: Karl Marx
people.description: Examined through class, labour, ideology, material power, and social transformation.

people.name: Søren Kierkegaard
people.description: Represents inwardness, choice, anxiety, faith, and critique of system.

people.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
people.description: Engaged through morality, power, genealogy, perspectivism, and self-creation.

people.name: Edmund Husserl
people.description: Represents disciplined description of experience and intentionality.

people.name: Martin Heidegger
people.description: An interlocutor on being, time, finitude, and the historical condition of understanding.

people.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
people.description: Examined through freedom, responsibility, bad faith, and social situation.

people.name: William James
people.description: Represents an inquiry into experience, consequences, truth, and pluralism.

people.name: John Dewey
people.description: Links inquiry with education, public life, democracy, and experimental intelligence.

people.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
people.description: Engaged through language, use, limits, rules, and forms of life.

people.name: Karl Popper
people.description: Represents criticism, falsifiability, open inquiry, and institutional error correction.

people.name: Thomas Kuhn
people.description: An interlocutor on paradigms, normal science, crisis, and scientific change.

people.name: M. K. Gandhi
people.description: Examined through nonviolence, truth, means, decentralization, and the limits of moral politics.

people.name: B. R. Ambedkar
people.description: Central to the critique of caste, constitutional morality, dignity, equality, and social democracy.

people.name: John Rawls
people.description: An interlocutor on fairness, basic liberties, institutions, and distributive justice.

people.name: Michel Foucault
people.description: Used critically to examine classification, institutions, knowledge, discipline, and silencing.

people.name: Jürgen Habermas
people.description: An interlocutor on communication, legitimacy, public reasoning, and democracy.

people.name: Antonio Gramsci
people.description: Supports analysis of cultural authority, common sense, hegemony, and counter-tradition.

people.name: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
people.description: Engaged in the archive's discussion of representation, subalternity, translation, and voice.

people.name: Homi K. Bhabha
people.description: Provides concepts for hybridity, cultural translation, and the ambivalence of authority.

people.name: Edward Said
people.description: An interlocutor on representation, canon, cultural power, and the geography of knowledge.

people.name: Judith Butler
people.description: Engaged in discussions of gender, performativity, recognition, vulnerability, and power.

people.name: Hélène Cixous
people.description: Used within the Parallel History's synthesis of feminist approaches to voice and writing.

people.name: Bertolt Brecht
people.description: A comparative framework for political theatre, estrangement, and critical spectatorship.

people.name: Augusto Boal
people.description: Supports the idea of participatory theatre from below and performance as social inquiry.

people.name: Antonin Artaud
people.description: An interlocutor in comparative accounts of body, intensity, ritual, and performance.

people.name: Jerzy Grotowski
people.description: A comparative figure for actor-centred, materially spare, and disciplined performance.

people.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
people.description: Provides a vocabulary for dialogism, heteroglossia, genre, and multiple social voices.

people.name: Walter Benjamin
people.description: An interlocutor on memory, fragments, reproduction, history, and the politics of the archive.

people.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
people.description: Engaged through interpretation, historical situatedness, dialogue, and horizons of understanding.

people.name: Lawrence Venuti
people.description: Supports reflection on visibility, domestication, foreignization, and translator responsibility.

people.name: A. K. Ramanujan
people.description: A comparative figure for multilingual literary worlds, translation, folklore, and context-sensitive reading.

people.name: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o
people.description: An interlocutor on language choice, cultural power, education, and decolonizing the mind.

people.name: Pierre Bourdieu
people.description: Supports analysis of fields, cultural capital, institutions, and canon formation.
